Actually array elements must be distinct (they said array of distinct positive integers). So you cannot have duplicate elements; thus you cannot have two copies of same x, but you also cannot have distinct elements x and y such that x + y = k. Since all elements distinct, even if x = k/2, you can't have two copies. So including x = k/2 is allowed because you can't pick the same element twice. However you need to check: If x = k/2 and k even, then having just one copy of x is fine because you need distinct pair sum to k: you would need another element equal to x to sum to k. Since no duplicate, it's safe.

Thus constraint: For any x in set, k - x cannot be also in set unless x == k - x and we only have at most one copy (so still ok). Actually if x == k - x (i.e., x = k/2), then the pair would need two copies of x, which we don't have. So including x = k/2 is allowed.

Thus the condition reduces to: The set cannot contain both x and k-x for any x < k - x (i.e., x != k/2). Equivalent: For each unordered pair (x, k-x) with x < k-x, you can pick at most one of them. For the special case x = k/2 (when k even), you can pick it at most once (but you can pick it, as it doesn't conflict with itself because you need distinct elements). So treat it as a "singleton" that can be taken.

Thus we want to select n distinct positive integers minimizing sum, while respecting that for each pair (x, k-x) we can pick at most one.
